Consumer BIA devices are highly reliable (precision error 0.0-0.49%) but inaccurate for tracking: against a four-compartment model the standard error for CHANGE in body fat was 1.7-2.6 percentage points. Unstandardised conditions (food, fluid, prior exercise) blunt or exaggerate measured change with most methods. Circumference-plus-skinfold estimates of thigh muscle CSA had ICC 0.96-0.98 and tracked 8 weeks of training in a pattern similar to pQCT while underestimating absolute size. A sports nutrition review concludes skinfolds are the method least affected by day-to-day variability.
body_measurements.practical_rule: Keep body measures optional, taken by the same person, same site, same time of day and fasted state, and show trends over many weeks. Ignore differences between two single readings that lie within the method's error (about 2 percentage points for a change in scale body fat); for girths no verified threshold was found, so rely on the trend only.
body_measurements.applied_as: A strictly optional log: trends only, shown from two values on and labelled as a rough trend; differences within the method's error (about 2 percentage points for body fat from a scale) are not interpreted. The AI sees relative changes only.

references.authors: Ulijaszek SJ, Kerr DA
references.title: Anthropometric measurement error and the assessment of nutritional status
references.key_finding: Review of anthropometric measurement error (TEM, %TEM, reliability R): weight and height are most precise; waist and hip circumference show strong between-observer differences and should where possible be taken by one observer; skinfolds can carry such large error that interpretation is problematic; R > 0.95 should be sought. An erratum exists.

references.authors: Siedler MR, Rodriguez C, Stratton MT, et al.
references.title: Assessing the reliability and cross-sectional and longitudinal validity of fifteen bioelectrical impedance analysis devices
references.key_finding: 73 adults, 15 BIA devices (14 consumer-grade) vs a four-compartment model; 37 returned after 12-16 weeks. Precision error 0.0-0.49%; cross-sectional constant error -3.5 to +11.7% body fat; for CHANGE, constant error -0.4 to +1.3% with standard error of the estimate 1.7-2.6% and concordance 0.37-0.78.

references.authors: Tinsley GM, Harty PS, Stratton MT, et al.
references.title: Tracking changes in body composition: comparison of methods and influence of pre-assessment standardisation
references.key_finding: Resistance-trained men, 6 weeks of training with a hyperenergetic diet, multiple methods under standardised and unstandardised conditions. Most methods showed meaningful errors when conditions were unstandardised, blunting or exaggerating true change; DXA and select digital anthropometry were more robust.

references.authors: DeFreitas JM, Beck TW, Stock MS, et al.
references.title: A comparison of techniques for estimating training-induced changes in muscle cross-sectional area
references.key_finding: 25 untrained men, 8 weeks of training. Two circumference-plus-skinfold equations for thigh muscle CSA had ICCs of 0.983 and 0.961 but significantly underestimated CSA vs pQCT; the error was consistent, so they showed increases with a pattern similar to pQCT. An erratum exists.

references.authors: Kasper AM, Langan-Evans C, Hudson JF, et al.
references.title: Come Back Skinfolds, All Is Forgiven: A Narrative Review of the Efficacy of Common Body Composition Methods in Applied Sports Practice
references.key_finding: Narrative review of body composition methods in applied sport: DXA is preferred when bone or limb-specific estimates are needed but requires control of food intake, prior exercise and hydration; across methods, skinfolds appear the least affected by day-to-day variability.

references.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Nickerson BS, Wilborn CD, et al.
references.title: Comparison of Multifrequency Bioelectrical Impedance vs. Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry for Assessing Body Composition Changes After Participation in a 10-Week Resistance Training Program
references.key_finding: 21 young men, 10-week programme. Mean changes did not differ between multifrequency BIA and DXA (fat mass -1.13 vs -1.19 kg; fat-free mass 0.10 vs 0.37 kg; SEE 1.0 kg and 1.5 kg), but the two methods were poor predictors of each other for segmental changes.

progression.title: Progression steps
progression.statement: Position stands recommend increasing the load only once the current workload is mastered: 2-10 % when one to two repetitions more than the target are possible (ACSM 2009). The 2026 ACSM stand lists training to fatigue, time under tension and periodization among the variables without a consistent effect on outcomes, and puts consistency of training first.
progression.practical_rule: Earn the step: first finish the set, then raise the target - in small increments.
progression.applied_as: A step of 1-3 % per session (the athlete's own rate on comparable days) only when the exercise is progressing AND the last set reached the effort target; otherwise the same force with full effort. The app stays at the lower end of the 2-10 % range because force is measured exactly and sessions are frequent. No steps for minors, on a 'maintain' profile or on a day with a moderate or poor check-in.
progression.arx_caveat: On a machine without an external load a 'step' is a target force, not a weight; the recommendation is transferred by analogy.

references.authors: American College of Sports Medicine
references.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
references.key_finding: When training at a specific RM load, a 2-10 % increase in load is recommended when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

references.authors: Currier BS, D'Souza AC, Singh MAF, et al.
references.title: American College of Sports Medicine Position Stand. Resistance Training Prescription for Muscle Function, Hypertrophy, and Physical Performance in Healthy Adults: An Overview of Reviews
references.key_finding: ACSM Position Stand 2026, overview of 137 systematic reviews (>30,000 participants), updating the 2009 stand. Strength was enhanced by loads >=80% 1RM, full range of motion, 2-3 sets, placement at the beginning of the session and >=2 sessions/week; hypertrophy by higher volumes (>=10 sets/week) and eccentric overload. Training to momentary fatigue, equipment type, set structure, time under tension and periodization did not consistently affect outcomes.

split_vs_full_body.title: Full-body sessions or a split by muscle groups
split_vs_full_body.statement: A 2024 systematic review with meta-analysis (14 studies, 392 subjects) found that split and full-body routines produce similar strength gains (bench press MD 1.19, p = 0.34; lower limb MD 2.47, p = 0.29) and similar muscle growth (elbow extensors, elbow flexors, vastus lateralis, lean body mass: all p > 0.8) when volume is equated; the authors conclude that people are free to choose by preference. Single trials agree: in 50 untrained women a 4-day upper/lower split and a 2-day full-body programme with the same weekly sets gave the same strength (bench press +30.0 % vs +25.5 %), power and muscle mass gains over 12 weeks; in 67 untrained subjects training a muscle twice (A/B split) or four times a week (full body) gave similar results at equal weekly sets. One 10-week trial in 21 trained men found a small edge of full body for one strength measure and of the split for thigh muscle thickness.
split_vs_full_body.practical_rule: At equal weekly volume it makes no difference whether the body is trained as a whole or in parts - choose what fits the week. A split allows training on consecutive days (different muscles work), shorter sessions and more sets for a muscle within one session; full body reaches everything with fewer visits.
split_vs_full_body.applied_as: Profile option 'how sessions are built': Automatic (1-2 sessions a week = full body, from 3 a rotating split), Full body, or Split by groups. A split here follows the machine's movement groups Push / Pull / Drive, so every helper muscle stays with the exercises it helps in; rest is still counted per muscle, which is what makes consecutive days possible. 'Next session only ...' lets the athlete pick the groups for a single session. When the chosen structure cannot deliver the asked number of sessions, the plan says so.
split_vs_full_body.arx_caveat: The trials equate volume with several sets per exercise. With ONE set per exercise the practical difference between the structures is weekly volume: more sessions mean more hard sets per muscle per week - that, not the structure itself, is what can add results.

references.authors: Ramos-Campo DJ, Benito-Peinado PJ, Andreu-Caravaca L, Rojo-Tirado MA, Rubio-Arias JÁ
references.title: Efficacy of Split Versus Full-Body Resistance Training on Strength and Muscle Growth: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
references.key_finding: 14 studies, 392 subjects: similar strength gains and muscle growth after split and full-body routines when volume is equated; individuals are free to select a routine based on personal preference.

references.authors: Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Schoenfeld BJ, Iversen VM, Cumming KT, Jensen S, Saeterbakken AH, Andersen V
references.title: A randomized trial on the efficacy of split-body versus full-body resistance training in non-resistance trained women
references.key_finding: 50 untrained women, 12 weeks, same exercises and weekly sets: full body twice a week vs upper/lower split four times a week - no between-group differences in strength, power or muscle mass.

references.authors: Evangelista AL, Braz TV, La Scala Teixeira CV, Rica RL, Alonso AC, Barbosa WA, Reis VM, Baker JS, Schoenfeld BJ, Bocalini DS, Greve JMD
references.title: Split or full-body workout routine: which is best to increase muscle strength and hypertrophy?
references.key_finding: 67 untrained subjects, 8 weeks: training a muscle twice a week (A/B split) or four times a week (full body) has similar effects on strength and muscle thickness, provided weekly set volume is equal.

references.authors: Bartolomei S, Nigro F, Malagoli Lanzoni I, Masina F, Di Michele R, Hoffman JR
references.title: A Comparison Between Total Body and Split Routine Resistance Training Programs in Trained Men
references.key_finding: 21 trained men, 10 weeks: both routines improved all strength and muscle thickness measures; slow isokinetic bench press improved more with total body (p = 0.015), vastus lateralis thickness more with the split routine (p = 0.037).

training_breaks.title: Training breaks: what is lost, what comes back, how to restart
training_breaks.statement: Stopping resistance training reduces every component of muscular performance, and the loss grows with the length of the break (meta-analysis of 103 studies: maximal force SMD -0.46; larger in people over 65 and in previously inactive people). Short breaks are harmless: in a 24-week RCT young men who trained in 6-week blocks separated by 3-week breaks ended with the same muscle size and strength as the group that trained without a break, because the retraining blocks produced faster gains. After a 10-week break strength and muscle size had decreased significantly, but they were regained within the first 5 weeks of retraining, and periodic and continuous training ended equal (RCT, 42 completers). After 20 weeks without training muscle size was back at baseline while strength stayed elevated. In older adults muscle size was not significantly reduced after 12-24 weeks without training, but clearly after 31-52 weeks. The protection against eccentric muscle damage (repeated-bout effect) lasts at least 6 months and is lost between 9 and 12 months; a light eccentric session a few days before a demanding one reduces its damage markedly (nine muscle groups: peak soreness 36-54 % lower). No trial shows that extra volume or extra sessions after a break bring the lost level back faster than normal training does.
training_breaks.practical_rule: A break of up to about three weeks needs no special treatment: continue the plan. After a longer break expect lower numbers in the first session, take them as the new starting point and progress from there - what was lost returns much faster than it was built. Do not try to catch up with extra sets, extra sessions or harder sessions. After six months or more, restart the eccentric side like a beginner: a controlled, sub-maximal first session protects against the damage of the next hard one.
training_breaks.applied_as: More than 14 days without training: the plan names the break, the first session back gets no progression step (numbers are held) and the date is no longer justified with the weekly rhythm. 28 days or more without direct work for an exercise's muscles: the old reference is only an orientation, the value reached becomes the new baseline, and the AI coach may set the target up to 15 % lower. An exercise not done for 180 days or more restarts at moderate effort without a target. The session after a break is built like any other - everything is recovered, so the big push, pull and leg exercise come first; full body or split still follows the sessions per week the athlete wants, not the break. When the athlete's real attendance in the four weeks up to the last session is too low for a split (a muscle would wait longer than about 8 days), the plan falls back to fuller sessions and says why. The load chapter no longer warns of strength loss after 10 days: up to about three weeks it says that nothing is lost but also nothing gained.
training_breaks.arx_caveat: All trials used conventional weights and mostly young or untrained subjects; none tested a motor-driven machine with eccentric overload. The 14- and 28-day thresholds are planner defaults inside what the trials show (3 weeks harmless, 10 weeks a clear but quickly reversible loss), not measured cut-offs.

references.authors: Bosquet L, Berryman N, Dupuy O, et al.
references.title: Effect of training cessation on muscular performance: a meta-analysis
references.key_finding: 103 studies. Stopping resistance training reduced submaximal strength (SMD -0.62), maximal force (SMD -0.46) and maximal power (SMD -0.20). The loss grew with the duration of the break (dose-response), was larger in people over 65 and, for maximal force and power, larger in inactive people than in recreational athletes.

references.authors: Ogasawara R, Yasuda T, Ishii N, Abe T
references.title: Comparison of muscle hypertrophy following 6-month of continuous and periodic strength training
references.key_finding: 14 young men, bench press 3 days/week for 24 weeks: continuous training vs three 6-week blocks separated by 3-week breaks. Overall gains in muscle cross-sectional area and 1RM were similar; in the second break / retraining cycle the periodic group gained significantly more than the continuous group in the same period.

references.authors: Halonen EJ, Gabriel I, Kelahaara MM, et al.
references.title: Does Taking a Break Matter-Adaptations in Muscle Strength and Size Between Continuous and Periodic Resistance Training
references.key_finding: 55 untrained adults randomised (42 completers, 45 % women), whole-body training twice a week: 10 weeks training, 10 weeks break, 10 weeks retraining vs 20 weeks continuous. 1RM, muscle cross-sectional area and jump height decreased during the break (p<0.05); in the first 5 weeks of retraining leg-press 1RM and muscle size rose faster than in the continuous group (p<0.01); both groups ended with similar adaptations.

references.authors: Grgic J
references.title: Use It or Lose It? A Meta-Analysis on the Effects of Resistance Training Cessation (Detraining) on Muscle Size in Older Adults
references.journal: Int J Environ Res Public Health
references.key_finding: 6 studies in older adults, training 9-24 weeks, detraining 12-52 weeks. Muscle size decreased after training cessation (d -0.83); the decrease was not significant after 12-24 weeks (d -0.60, CI -1.21 to 0.01) and significant after 31-52 weeks (d -1.11).

references.authors: Psilander N, Eftestøl E, Cumming KT, et al.
references.title: Effects of training, detraining, and retraining on strength, hypertrophy, and myonuclear number in human skeletal muscle
references.key_finding: 19 adults: 10 weeks of unilateral strength training, 20 weeks of detraining, 5 weeks of bilateral retraining. Muscle thickness and fibre cross-sectional area returned to baseline during detraining while strength remained elevated (a long-lasting motor learning effect). The previously trained leg did not respond better to retraining; myonuclear number had not increased with training, so the study was no rigorous test of the muscle-memory hypothesis.

references.authors: Nosaka K, Sakamoto K, Newton M, Sacco P
references.title: How long does the protective effect on eccentric exercise-induced muscle damage last?
references.key_finding: 35 men, two bouts of maximal eccentric elbow-flexor exercise 6, 9 or 12 months apart: the repeated-bout effect (faster strength recovery, less soreness, smaller CK and swelling) lasted at least 6 months for most markers and was lost between 9 and 12 months.

references.authors: Huang MJ, Nosaka K, Wang HS, et al.
references.title: Damage protective effects conferred by low-intensity eccentric contractions on arm, leg and trunk muscles
references.key_finding: 24 untrained young men, nine muscle groups: 50 eccentric contractions at 10 % of maximal isometric strength two days before 50 contractions at 80 %. With the light session first, strength recovered faster (6-31 % greater at day 5), peak soreness was 36-54 % lower and the rises in CK and myoglobin were far smaller.

references.authors: Chen TC, Tseng WC, Huang GL, et al.
references.title: Low-intensity eccentric contractions attenuate muscle damage induced by subsequent maximal eccentric exercise of the knee extensors in the elderly
references.key_finding: 26 healthy men aged about 66: low-intensity eccentric knee-extensor contractions (10 % of isometric strength) caused no measurable change and, performed 7 days before maximal eccentric exercise, led to smaller strength loss, faster recovery and less soreness than without them.

range_of_motion.title: Range of motion: when force values are comparable, and what a shorter range trains
range_of_motion.statement: Muscle force depends on the position in the range (length-tension and leverage), and adaptations are specific to the muscle length trained: isometric training at long muscle lengths produced more hypertrophy than equal volumes at short lengths (systematic review of 26 studies), and full-ROM resistance training produced greater strength (ES 0.56) and lower-limb hypertrophy (ES 0.88) than partial ROM (meta-analysis of 16 studies). A peak-force measurement itself scatters from day to day: on an isokinetic dynamometer with identical positioning the typical error of peak torque was 8-17 % (averaged measures 8-10 %) despite good relative reliability (ICC 0.84-0.94).
range_of_motion.practical_rule: Compare force only between sets performed over the same range. A range difference far below the day-to-day scatter of the measurement is the same set-up; a clearly shorter range is a different exercise for comparison purposes - and less stimulus at the stretched end, so it should be a deliberate choice, not drift.
range_of_motion.applied_as: A training day is comparable when its range of motion lies within ROM_TOLERANCE (10 %) of the exercise's reference range (the range most of the last ROM_REF_DAYS days agree on). On a 30 cm press that is 3 cm: a shift of at most a tenth of the range at one end, which touches the peak only if the peak lies at that very end, and below the scatter of a peak measurement itself. Days outside the band stay in the charts (hollow markers, a warning) but feed neither trend, personal best, delta nor targets; the same band decides last-vs-previous comparisons and the pair / order effects.
range_of_motion.arx_caveat: No study measured force-position behaviour on a motor-driven adaptive machine; the reliability figures come from an isokinetic dynamometer in older men and the ROM studies concern training adaptations with conventional loads. The 10 % band is a measurement convention (v0.9.2; 5 % before), not a tested value - in the owner's own data the range between days is either identical (0 %) or clearly different (17 % and more), so both bands have always separated the same days.

references.authors: Pallarés JG, Hernández-Belmonte A, Martínez-Cava A, et al.
references.title: Effects of range of motion on resistance training adaptations: A systematic review and meta-analysis
references.key_finding: 16 studies. Full-ROM training produced greater muscle strength (ES 0.56) and lower-limb hypertrophy (ES 0.88) than partial ROM; functional performance favoured full ROM without reaching significance; no difference for muscle thickness, pennation angle or fascicle length.

references.authors: Oranchuk DJ, Storey AG, Nelson AR, Cronin JB
references.title: Isometric training and long-term adaptations: Effects of muscle length, intensity, and intent: A systematic review
references.key_finding: 26 research outputs. Isometric training at longer muscle lengths produced greater hypertrophy (0.86-1.69 %/week) than equal volumes at shorter lengths (0.08-0.83 %/week); adaptations are specific to the trained muscle length, i.e. force capacity is position-dependent.

references.authors: Symons TB, Vandervoort AA, Rice CL, et al.
references.title: Reliability of a single-session isokinetic and isometric strength measurement protocol in older men
references.journal: J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci
references.key_finding: 19 men (72 +/- 5 y), Biodex, two test days, identical positioning. ICC 0.84-0.94 (good relative reliability), but the typical error as a coefficient of variation was 8-10 % for averaged torque and 8-17 % for single peak torque - the day-to-day scatter of a peak-force number even without any change of range.
